    import argparse, base58
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--d', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    enc1 = base58.b58encode(args.a.encode())
    enc2 = base58.b58encode(args.b.encode())
    dec1 = base58.b58decode(args.c)
    dec2 = base58.b58decode(args.d)
    print(enc1); print(enc2); print(dec1); print(dec2)

Goal: a Node.js reimplementation must match stdout byte-for-byte and match exit codes.
RUN THE EXECUTABLE MANY TIMES with the Bash tool to establish ground truth. Do NOT use the
`python` command (unavailable/forbidden). Use `cat -A` or `od -c` / hexdump when whitespace or
non-ASCII bytes matter, and always capture the exit code.
Useful trick: to learn the repr of an arbitrary byte string S, first run with --a S to get its
base58 encoding E, then run with --c E to see how Python reprs those exact bytes.
Be rigorous and adversarial: try to break your own hypotheses. Report ONLY what you verified by running.

YOUR DIMENSION: Python's `print(bytes_object)` output format, i.e. bytes repr.
Determine EXACTLY, with evidence, how each byte class is rendered inside b'...':
 - printable ASCII 0x20..0x7e
 - the single quote 0x27 and the double quote 0x22, including which quote character Python
   chooses to delimit the literal when the payload contains ' only, " only, both, or neither
 - backslash 0x5c
 - 0x09 tab, 0x0a newline, 0x0d carriage return
 - other C0 control bytes (0x00..0x08, 0x0b, 0x0c, 0x0e..0x1f) and 0x7f
 - high bytes 0x80..0xff
 - is hex in \xNN lower or upper case? is it always exactly 2 digits?
 - empty bytes
Construct payloads that contain these bytes by the --a then --c round-trip trick described above.
E.g. to see repr of "it's": run --a "it's" to get base58 E, then --c E.
Cover at minimum: a payload with only ', a payload with only ", a payload with BOTH ' and ",
a payload with a backslash, a payload with tab+newline+CR, a payload with 0x00 and 0x1f and 0x7f,
a payload with 0x80 and 0xff (use UTF-8 multibyte input like 'é' or '€' to generate high bytes),
and the empty payload.
Produce a complete, unambiguous escaping algorithm as rules.

input.dimension: Python `print(bytes_object)` output format (bytes repr) as emitted by /workspace/dataset/test15_executable
rules:
Every one of the 4 printed values is a Python `bytes` object rendered by `repr()`, followed by exactly one 0x0a newline (verified: `od -c` shows `b ' Z d i 9 ' 
 b ' Z d L 5 ' 
 b " ' " 
 b ' " ' 
`, 4 lines, no trailing blank line, no CRLF). Exit code 0 on success.
The literal always begins with a lowercase ASCII `b` (0x62) immediately followed by the chosen delimiter quote, and ends with the same delimiter. No `rb`/`B` prefix, no spaces.

DELIMITER SELECTION (exact rule): let q = 0x27 (') present in the byte string, and d = 0x22 (") present. If q is true AND d is false -> delimiter is 0x22 ("). In every other case (neither present, only " present, or BOTH present) -> delimiter is 0x27 ('). Verified: b"it's" (' only), b'"dq"' (" only), b'a\'b"c' (both -> single-quote delim), b'abc'/b'' (neither).

QUOTE ESCAPING: the 0x27 byte is escaped as backslash+apostrophe (\') if and only if the delimiter is 0x27; otherwise it is emitted raw. The 0x22 byte is NEVER escaped (it is always emitted raw as `"`), because the " delimiter is only chosen when no 0x22 byte exists. Verified: hex 2722 -> b'\'"' ; hex 2227 -> b'"\'' ; hex 2227275c -> b'"\'\'\\' ; 200x 0x27 -> b"''''...''" (204 output bytes = 1 b + 1 quote + 200 raw quotes + 1 quote + 1 newline, i.e. one byte each, no escapes, no truncation/wrapping).

BACKSLASH 0x5c is ALWAYS escaped as two bytes `\\`, regardless of which delimiter was chosen. Verified: hex 5c -> b'\\' ; hex 5c27 -> b"\\'" (double-quote delim, backslash still doubled) ; hex 5c22 -> b'\\"' ; 'back\slash' -> b'back\\slash'.

SHORT ESCAPES: exactly three bytes get a letter escape: 0x09 -> `	`, 0x0a -> `
`, 0x0d -> ``. Verified: hex 09090a -> b'		
' ; hex 0d0a -> b'
' ; payload $'	
' -> b'	
'.

NO OTHER LETTER ESCAPES EXIST. 0x07 is NOT `\a`, 0x08 is NOT `\b`, 0x0b is NOT `\v`, 0x0c is NOT `\f`, 0x00 is NOT `\0`. They all use hex form. Verified in the full 0x00..0xff sweep: `...\x06\x07\x08\t\n\x0b\x0c\r\x0e...` and hex 0b0c -> b'\x0b\x0c'.

PRINTABLE ASCII 0x20..0x7e are emitted as their raw single byte, with the only exceptions being 0x27 (conditionally escaped per the delimiter rule) and 0x5c (always doubled). Space 0x20 is raw. Verified by feeding the full 0x20..0x7e range: `od -c` of the output line shows ` ! " # $ % & \ ' ( ) * + , - . / 0-9 : ; < = > ? @ A-Z [ \ \ ] ^ _ ` a-z { | } ~` i.e. only ' and \ gained a backslash.

ALL OTHER BYTES use the form backslash + lowercase `x` + EXACTLY 2 lowercase hex digits, zero-padded. This covers 0x00-0x08, 0x0b, 0x0c, 0x0e-0x1f, 0x7f, and 0x80-0xff. Never 1 digit, never 3+, never `\u`/`\U`/octal, never uppercase X or uppercase A-F. Verified single bytes: b'\x00', b'\x1f', b'\x7f', b'\x80', b'\xff'; and the exhaustive 0x00..0xff sweep shows \x0b \x8a \x9f \xab \xcd \xef \xfa \xff all lowercase and 2-digit.

Complete rendering table for a byte n (given chosen delimiter Q): n==0x5c -> '\\\\'; n==0x09 -> '\\t'; n==0x0a -> '\\n'; n==0x0d -> '\\r'; n==0x27 and Q==0x27 -> "\\'"; 0x20 <= n <= 0x7e -> String.fromCharCode(n); else -> '\\x' + n.toString(16).padStart(2,'0')  (lowercase).
EMPTY BYTES render as exactly `b''` (single quotes, 4 bytes plus newline). Verified: running with --a '' --b '' --c '' --d '' produced four lines of `b''` and exit code 0.

The two encode outputs (enc1/enc2) are also bytes objects and therefore also printed with the `b'...'` wrapper; since the base58 alphabet is `123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz` (no quote, no backslash, no non-printables) they always render as b' + raw alphabet chars + '. Empty input yields b''.

The repr is a single physical line no matter how long the byte string is: newlines inside the data become the two-character `\n`, and there is no length-based truncation or line wrapping (verified with a 200-byte payload producing a 204-byte single line).
